text_elements: Bottom-up: from n singleton clusters to one root
Start with n clusters (one per point). At each step, merge the two clusters with smallest linkage distance δ(A,B). Repeat n−1 times until one cluster remains. The merge history is the dendrogram.

Villages on a hillside build a road to their nearest neighbour and merge into one settlement. Settlements keep merging until the whole hillside is one township. The order and 'road lengths' built = exactly the dendrogram.
No need to fix K in advance
Produces a full hierarchy of clusterings
O(n²) memory — limited to small/medium n
slides.full_text:
Agglomerative Clustering — Concept & Intuition
Bottom-up: from n singleton clusters to one root
CONCEPT
Start with n clusters (one per point). At each step, merge the two clusters with smallest linkage distance δ(A,B). Repeat n−1 times until one cluster remains. The merge history is the dendrogram.
INTUITION
Villages on a hillside build a road to their nearest neighbour and merge into one settlement. Settlements keep merging until the whole hillside is one township. The order and 'road lengths' built = exactly the dendrogram.
Key Properties
▸  
No need to fix K in advance
▸  
Produces a full hierarchy of clusterings
▸  
Deterministic — no random initialisation
▸  
O(n²) memory — limited to small/medium n
▸  
Monotone merge heights (usually)

text_elements: The merge rule and dendrogram definition
Merge Rule (applied at every step t):
(A*, B*) = argmin δ(A,B)   over all A ≠ B in current partition Pₜ
Each step removes the merged pair and inserts their union as one new cluster — reducing the partition size by exactly 1.
If v is ancestor of u in T:  h(v) ≥ h(u)
Merge heights never decrease as we go up the tree. Single/Complete/Average/Ward all satisfy this; centroid/median linkage can violate it (inversions).
Complexity: O(n³) naive  |  O(n² log n) with priority queue  |  O(n²) memory — the key scalability constraint
slides.full_text:
Mathematical Formulation
The merge rule and dendrogram definition
Merge Rule (applied at every step t):
(A*, B*) = argmin δ(A,B)   over all A ≠ B in current partition Pₜ
Transition Rule
Pₜ₊₁ = (Pₜ \ {A*,B*}) ∪ {A* ∪ B*}
Each step removes the merged pair and inserts their union as one new cluster — reducing the partition size by exactly 1.
Monotonicity Property
If v is ancestor of u in T:  h(v) ≥ h(u)
Merge heights never decrease as we go up the tree. Single/Complete/Average/Ward all satisfy this; centroid/median linkage can violate it (inversions).
Complexity: O(n³) naive  |  O(n² log n) with priority queue  |  O(n²) memory — the key scalability constraint

text_elements: Two clusters are 'close' if even ONE point from each is close — like crowds judged near if a single pair of people touch. Highly sensitive to bridging points; causes chaining (long, stringy clusters).
Best for: elongated / non-convex shapes (e.g. moon-shaped data)
slides.full_text:
Linkage 1 — Single Linkage (Nearest Neighbour)
FORMULA
δ_single(A,B) = min { ‖a−b‖ : a∈A, b∈B }
Intuition
Two clusters are 'close' if even ONE point from each is close — like crowds judged near if a single pair of people touch. Highly sensitive to bridging points; causes chaining (long, stringy clusters).
Best for: elongated / non-convex shapes (e.g. moon-shaped data)
Worked Trace (this dataset)
Step 1: d(A,B)=2 → merge {A,B}, h=2
Step 2: d(C,D)=2 → merge {C,D}, h=2
Step 3: d({CD},E)=min(8,6)=6 → merge, h=6
Step 4: d({AB},{CDE})=min(6,6)=6 → merge, h=6
7

text_elements: Two clusters are only 'close' if EVERY pair across them is reasonably close — the pessimistic, worst-case view. Discourages chaining; produces tight, compact, equal-sized clusters. Sensitive to single outliers.
Best for: tight, well-separated, roughly equal-sized groups
slides.full_text:
Linkage 2 — Complete Linkage (Farthest Neighbour)
FORMULA
δ_complete(A,B) = max { ‖a−b‖ : a∈A, b∈B }
Intuition
Two clusters are only 'close' if EVERY pair across them is reasonably close — the pessimistic, worst-case view. Discourages chaining; produces tight, compact, equal-sized clusters. Sensitive to single outliers.
Best for: tight, well-separated, roughly equal-sized groups
Worked Trace (this dataset)
Step 1: d(A,B)=2 → merge {A,B}, h=2
Step 2: d(C,D)=2 → merge {C,D}, h=2
Step 3: d({CD},E)=max(8,6)=8 → merge, h=8
Step 4: d({AB},{CDE})=max(10,16)=16 → merge, h=16
8

text_elements: Instead of an extreme (closest or farthest pair), average EVERY cross-cluster pair. A balanced compromise between single linkage's chaining and complete linkage's outlier sensitivity.
Best for: general-purpose default when no shape assumption favours an extreme
slides.full_text:
Linkage 3 — Average Linkage (UPGMA)
FORMULA
δ_avg(A,B) = (1/|A||B|) · Σ_a Σ_b ‖a−b‖
Intuition
Instead of an extreme (closest or farthest pair), average EVERY cross-cluster pair. A balanced compromise between single linkage's chaining and complete linkage's outlier sensitivity.
Best for: general-purpose default when no shape assumption favours an extreme
Worked Trace (this dataset)
Step 1: d(A,B)=2 → merge {A,B}, h=2
Step 2: d(C,D)=2 → merge {C,D}, h=2
Step 3: d({CD},E)=½(8+6)=7 → merge, h=7
Step 4: d({AB},{CDE})=62/6≈10.33 → merge
9

text_elements: Asks: 'if I merge these two clusters, how much does overall variance (WCSS) increase?' Always picks the least costly merge. Produces the most compact, K-Means-like clusters of any linkage.
Best for: general-purpose default; matches K-Means geometry — usually the top recommendation
slides.full_text:
Linkage 4 — Ward's Linkage (Minimum Variance)
FORMULA
ΔJ(A,B) = |A||B| / (|A|+|B|) · ‖μ_A − μ_B‖²
Intuition
Asks: 'if I merge these two clusters, how much does overall variance (WCSS) increase?' Always picks the least costly merge. Produces the most compact, K-Means-like clusters of any linkage.
Best for: general-purpose default; matches K-Means geometry — usually the top recommendation
Worked Trace (this dataset)
Step 1: ΔJ(A,B)=½(2)²=2 → h=√2≈1.41
Step 2: ΔJ(C,D)=2 → h=√2≈1.41
Step 3: ΔJ({CD},E)≈32.67 → h≈5.72
Step 4: ΔJ({AB},{CDE})≈128.1 → h≈11.32

text_elements: All Four Linkages — Side-by-Side on the SAME Data
Lance–Williams Recurrence (used by SciPy / scikit-learn internally)
δ(A∪B, C) = α_A·δ(A,C) + α_B·δ(B,C) + β·δ(A,B) + γ·|δ(A,C) − δ(B,C)|
Allows O(1) incremental distance updates after each merge — no need to revisit raw points. Coefficients (α_A, α_B, β, γ) differ per linkage.
All linkages agree on the first 2 merges (singleton distances) but diverge sharply once cluster sizes grow

text_elements: A dendrogram is a rooted binary tree whose n leaves are the data points and whose n−1 internal nodes are the successive merges. Each internal node's height equals the linkage distance at that merge.
Cutting Rule: a horizontal cut at height t partitions data into K(t) clusters = number of edges crossed by the line.
slides.full_text:
Constructing & Reading Dendrograms — Concept
CONCEPT
A dendrogram is a rooted binary tree whose n leaves are the data points and whose n−1 internal nodes are the successive merges. Each internal node's height equals the linkage distance at that merge.
Formal Definition
A dendrogram (T,h) satisfies:
1) h(leaf) = 0 for all leaves
2) Monotonicity: if v is ancestor
   of u, then h(v) ≥ h(u)
Cutting Rule: a horizontal cut at height t partitions data into K(t) clusters = number of edges crossed by the line.
Construction Algorithm
1. Create n leaves at height 0
2. For each merge (A*,B*,h):
   - locate subtree roots
   - create new internal node
     at height h joining them
3. Final node = root of T

text_elements: from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster
Z = linkage(X, method='ward')   # try: single / complete / average
slides.full_text:
Python Implementation — Linkages & Dendrogram
SciPy: linkage(), dendrogram(), fcluster()
import numpy as np
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
X = np.array([2, 4, 10, 12, 18]).reshape(-1, 1)
labels = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
Z = linkage(X, method='ward')   # try: single / complete / average
print(np.round(Z, 2))   # [idx1, idx2, height, cluster_size]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
dendrogram(Z, labels=labels, ax=ax, color_threshold=8)
ax.axhline(y=8, color='#B5621A', linestyle='--',
           label='Cut at h=8  ->  K=2')
ax.set_ylabel('Merge height (Ward distance)')
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# Extract flat clusters
flat = fcluster(Z, t=2, criterion='maxclust')
print(dict(zip(labels, flat)))

text_elements: Height of a join = dissimilarity at which those subtrees were merged. Taller joins mean more dissimilar groups were forced together.
The largest vertical gap with no horizontal crossing is the most natural place to cut — it suggests the most stable K.
Single linkage often shows gradual, staircase-like merges rather than one clear gap — making the cut harder to choose.
Complete and Ward linkage produce dendrograms with a few large, well-separated final merges — easy, confident cuts.
Trace down from the cut line to the leaves below each remaining subtree to recover exact membership.
If results look implausible, reconsider the linkage — chaining or excessive compactness are both diagnostic symptoms.

text_elements: Agglomerative clustering merges the two closest clusters at each of n−1 steps, producing a complete dendrogram.
Single (min) chains; Complete (max) is compact but outlier-sensitive; Average balances both; Ward minimises variance increase.
All linkages can be updated incrementally via the Lance–Williams recurrence — no need to revisit raw points.
A dendrogram encodes every possible flat clustering simultaneously; height = merge dissimilarity.
The optimal cut is typically the largest gap between consecutive merge heights.
O(n²) memory limits HAC to small/medium datasets — for large n, consider K-Means or DBSCAN instead.
